name: Vibravox
description: A GDPR-compliant dataset of French speech captured with five body-conduction audio sensors and one airborne reference microphone. It contains audio recordings of speech samples and physiological sounds from 188 participants under quiet and noisy acoustic conditions, with annotations about recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poiree, Veronique Zimpfer, Eric Bavu
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poiree, and E. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was built through a controlled recording protocol using six simultaneously recorded sensors worn by participants: five body-conduction microphones and one airborne reference microphone. Recordings were made with a Zoom F8n at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution, with a 20 Hz high-pass filter applied to each channel. For each participant, four consecutive recording steps were performed: speech-clean (15 minutes of reading French Wikipedia sentences), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds of silence while ambient noise was played through a 56-loudspeaker 3D spatializer), speechless-clean (54 seconds of silence in complete silence), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of reading in noisy conditions using in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events). A total of 200 participants contributed, and 188 were retained after post-processing.
rai:dataCollectionType: Direct measurement, Experiments, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous audio recordings from a headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone, and temple vibration pickup. Text prompts came from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise excerpts were sourced largely from AudioSet, with additional in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Textual data from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice were filtered to exclude most proper names, numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Text was normalized by lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated and manually corrected for some unrecognized words. Audio post-processing applied three automatic filters to speech-clean utterances based on phoneme error rate, speech-versus-silence SNR, and speech level versus mean silence level to remove mispronunciations, sensor shifts, malfunctions, and unequipped microphones. Voice activity detection timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides, and in rare boundary overflow cases audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The final dataset was split by speaker into train, validation, and test sets with 80%/10%/10% of male and female speakers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included applying a 20 Hz high-pass filter uniformly to each acquisition channel during recording. Text preprocessing included filtering unwanted sentences, lowercasing, and punctuation removal except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the CoML lab phonemizer and manually corrected for some words. For audio quality control, indicators were extracted using whisper-timestamped to align transcriptions and identify voiced and non-voiced segments, then automatic filters removed samples with phoneme error rate above 10%, SNR below 1.5 dB, or speech level not exceeding the sensor's mean silence level. Only filtered speech-clean samples were retained, and the other subsets were included if the participant had non-empty speech-clean data.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. Sentences read by participants were sourced from filtered French Wikipedia text. Corresponding phonetic transcriptions in IPA were generated using the CoML lab text phonemizer, and a manual phonetic transcription phase was used for some unrecognized words to preserve the minimal French phonetic alphabet.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors analyzed annotation quality by computing phoneme error rate between labeled phonetic transcriptions and phonetic transcriptions derived from Whisper output using Levenshtein distance. Samples with PER greater than 10% were discarded to address discrepancies between labeled transcription and actual pronunciation and ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab phonemizer, whisper-timestamped model based on Whisper
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants were collected or reported. The paper also mentions diverse morphologies and that all necessary GDPR measures were taken, including informed consent, anonymization, and encryption of data during storage and analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support development of robust communication systems for real-world applications, particularly communication in noisy environments. The paper discusses applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, intelligence gathering, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs such as heart rate.
rai:dataBiases: To increase representativeness and inclusivity, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants. The dataset was split with balanced male and female proportions across train, validation, and test. The paper also notes that one-size-fits-all in-ear designs can cause inadequate acoustic sealing for certain ear canal anatomies, affecting performance for some participants.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is in French, which limits language coverage. Post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences, prioritizing rigorous analysis and fair microphone comparison rather than maximizing overall performance. Some issues remained possible, such as rigid in-ear microphones failing to achieve proper acoustic sealing for small ear canals without triggering filters. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference for training. The paper also notes that existing and body-conducted data generally face bandwidth limitations, noise/artifact issues, and variability across sensors and participants.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and testing of speech-related tasks including speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. The speech-clean subset contains most of the training data and uses the airborne microphone as reference. The speech-noisy subset is mainly for testing because it lacks a clean reference. The speechless-noisy subset can be mixed with speech-clean for data augmentation to simulate noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference. The speechless-clean subset can be used for tasks such as heart rate tracking, analyzing sensor noise properties, or generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor noise.
